parts.title: Do Chinese counting words carry hidden numbers? A study of how people handle Chinese classifiers and measure words
parts.abstract: In Chinese, you cannot say "five apples". You must say "five [classifier] apples", where the classifier is a small word that sits between the number and the noun. There are two kinds of classifier. The first, which we call a sortal classifier (C), sorts objects into groups by what they are like. The second, which we call a measure word (M), also known as a "classifier" in English, tells you how much of something there is. Both kinds carry a mathematical value: a number that tells you how many of the basic unit are involved. We wanted to find out whether people actually use these values when they understand the words. To test this, we ran a language experiment in which people saw a phrase such as "one [classifier] apple" and had to pick which of two other phrases was closer in meaning to it. People were more accurate and faster with classifiers and measure words that have a fixed value than with those whose value can vary. These results show that mathematical values do play an important part in how people handle these words. Our study may therefore help explain how the way Chinese counts things shapes the way people think about size and amount.
parts.introduction_first: Chinese is a language that uses what we call numeral classifiers. Whenever you want to say how many of something there are, you need a word that stands for a unit of that thing. This word comes between the number and the noun. There are two kinds. The sortal classifier (C), also called a "classifier", sorts objects into groups by what they are like. The measure word (M), also called a "measure word", tells you how much of something there is. In Table 1, ben and ke are classifiers (C), while xiang (box) and da (dozen) are measure words (M). In this paper, we use C/M to mean both kinds together.
parts.introduction_rest:
Classifiers and measure words have a lot in common. They sit in the same place in a sentence, and you can never use one kind where the other is needed [1–3]. They also differ. A classifier describes the noun, while a measure word tells you how much of the noun there is [4–6]. Put more precisely, a classifier sorts a noun into a group by pointing out some important or built-in feature of it. A measure word, on the other hand, gives the amount of the thing the noun stands for [5,7]. Take the examples in Table 1. The classifier ben draws attention to the size of the object, and it can only be used for a bound copy of printed material, such as a book or a magazine. The measure word xiang means "a box of". It adds new information about how much of the noun there is, because a box can hold any amount of any object.

Her [8] brought these similarities and differences together with a new mathematical idea. In this idea, the link between the number and the classifier or measure word is multiplication. The difference between the two kinds is written exactly like this: [Num X N] = [[Num × X] N]. Here Num is the number, X is the word that goes between the number and the noun N, and the brackets show the order of the steps. The rule is simple: X is a classifier (C) if its mathematical value is 1, and X is a measure word (M) if its value is anything else.

Here are two examples. In shi ke pingguo ("ten C apples"), the number shi (ten) and the classifier ke work together as a multiplying pair, giving 10 × 1. In the same way, in shi da pingguo ("ten M-dozen apples"), the number shi (ten) and the measure word da (dozen) form a multiplying pair, giving 10 × 12. Seen this way, classifiers and measure words are alike because both are multiplied by the number. They sit in exactly the same place in the sentence, so they belong to a single grammatical group. They differ, though, in their built-in values: a classifier equals 1, while a measure word does not. That makes them two separate subgroups.

The number 1 has a special property. It is the only number that leaves everything unchanged when you multiply by it, so it adds nothing to the calculation. Any other value, whether a number or not, does add something. This special property of 1 may explain why classifiers can behave differently from measure words, even though they belong to one grammatical group [8].

Her and Wu [9] then sorted the values carried by classifiers and measure words into four groups, using two questions. Is the value a number or not? And is it fixed or can it vary? (See Table 2.) M1 and M2 both carry number values, but M1's values are fixed and M2's are not. M3 and M4 both carry values that are not numbers, but again M3's are fixed and M4's are not. So the classifier (C), M1 and M3 carry fixed values, while M2 and M4 do not.

M2 and M4 are alike in that their values are vague and not fixed. The difference is that the vague value of an M2 is a number, while the vague value of an M4 is not. For example, the M2 cuo ("small gang") must be followed by a count noun, such as yi cuo qiangdao ("a small gang of bandits"), and its value must be a number larger than one. In the same way, the M2 bang ("gang") in yi bang qiangdao ("a gang of bandits") must also have a value larger than two. However, bang usually suggests a bigger number than cuo does.

The vague values of M4 are different. They are not numbers. They can be length, area, weight, volume, time and so on. For example, the M4 di ("drop"), as in yi di shui ("a drop of water"), refers to a vague amount of water shaped like a teardrop. The M4 tan ("puddle"), as in yi tan shui ("a puddle of water"), also refers to a vague amount of water, but in a shape with no set form. A puddle is usually much bigger than a drop.

This is where things get interesting. In English, the words that match M2 and M4 are clearly nouns. In Chinese, however, M2 and M4 belong to their own grammatical group, the numeral classifiers [8]. People disagree about whether understanding Chinese numeral classifiers involves thinking about size and amount. Our study aimed to settle this question.

This theory is attractive, but there was no real-world evidence that people actually use the mathematical values of classifiers and measure words. So we ran a language experiment to find out whether people handle these words by their mathematical values, as the theory predicts they should. More specifically, the theory predicted that the gap between words with fixed values (C, M1 and M3) and words with vague values (M2 and M4) would stand out more than the gap between words with number values (C, M1 and M2) and words with non-number values (M3 and M4). The simple reason is this. A vague M2 or M4 cannot be forced into a single fixed value unless the surrounding conversation gives a clear, strong reason to do so. An M3 or M4, whose value is not a number, can quite easily be turned into a number by switching to a smaller unit, for example one kilo into one thousand grams.

The most relevant earlier study is by Cui and colleagues [10]. They used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a scan that shows which parts of the brain are active while someone does a task. They compared brain activity while people handled classifiers with activity while they handled tool nouns, numbers and dot arrays. Tool nouns are words for concrete objects used as tools, utensils or instruments, such as liandao (sickle) and laba (trumpet). The task asked people to compare how close two items were in meaning. For example, the word fuzi (axe) appeared at the top of the screen, and people had to decide which of two words shown at the bottom, liandao (sickle) or niezi (tweezers), was closer in meaning to fuzi.

For classifiers and tool nouns, the brain showed more activity in the left middle frontal gyrus (MTG) and the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), rather than in the right intraparietal sulcus (IPS), as it did for numbers and dot arrays. The IPS is a part of the brain that plays an important role in representing size and amount [11–12]. This result was rather unexpected under Her's theory [8], which predicts that handling classifiers and measure words should look more like handling numbers and dot arrays than like handling tool nouns. Some classifiers and measure words (see Table 2), along with numbers and dot arrays, carry a number value. So we expected that handling classifiers and measure words, but not tool nouns, would bring more activity in the right IPS.

One important reason why Cui and colleagues [10] did not find more IPS activity for classifiers and measure words than for tool nouns may be that their "classifiers" mixed classifiers and measure words together, so the two kinds were never told apart. Yet, as we described above, studies of language suggest that classifiers and measure words differ in important ways [e.g., 5–6]. Her and Wu's sorting [9] also splits the values of classifiers and measure words into fixed and variable. Presumably, words with a fixed value may be linked to exact numbers, while words with a variable value may be linked to rough estimates. We expected that when all the values were fixed, people would choose the classifier or measure word whose value was the same as, or closer to, the value of the target word. It was unclear, however, how people would handle words with variable values.

Cui and colleagues [10] also did not use complete phrases of the form [Num X N], such as yi zhang haibao ("1 C-flat poster, one poster"). Instead, they used phrases of the form [Num X], such as yi zhang ("1 C-flat"). This meant the surrounding meaning was not strictly limited. So we repeated the same kind of task as Cui and colleagues [10], but used a more suitable set of phrases, the complete [Num X N] phrases such as yi zhang haibao ("1 C-flat poster, one poster"), to test whether people handle classifiers and measure words by their mathematical values.

We expected two things. First, people would compare the mathematical values carried by the classifiers and measure words and choose the one whose value was the same as, or closer to, the target. Second, people would be more accurate with words that have fixed values than with words that have variable values.
parts.methods:
## Method

### Who took part

We recruited twenty people from National Chengchi University: 16 women and 4 men, aged 20 to 28. Their average age was 22.6 years, give or take 2.06 years. All of them were right-handed and had normal eyesight, or eyesight that was corrected to normal. Mandarin was their first language. The Research Ethics Committee of National Taiwan University approved the study. Each person gave written informed consent, meaning they agreed to take part after the study was explained to them, and each received NT$100.

### The phrases we used and how we set up the experiment

We tested two things at once, and each person took part in every version of the experiment. This is called a 2 × 2 within-subject design. The first thing was the type of word: a number word (C, M1 and M2) or a non-number word (M3 and M4). The second was whether the mathematical value was fixed or variable. The fixed-value words were C, M1 and M3, and the variable-value words were M2 and M4.

We had thirteen C/M words for each condition (see S1 Table). Each C/M word appeared twice as the target, the phrase at the top of the screen. For each trial, we also picked two other C/M words from the same condition to act as the answer and the distractor. A distractor is the wrong choice, placed there to test whether people really understand the meaning.

We built the phrases in pairs of three. For each set of three C/M words, two experimenters came up with a sensible noun to go with them, so that the meaning of the phrases was clear. One experimenter created the phrases, which follow the pattern [number word] [C/M] [noun]. The other checked that every phrase was clear and easy to understand. When a phrase was unclear, the two experimenters talked it over and chose a different noun that fitted the set of C/M words better. We never used the same noun twice during the experiment.

In the end, we had 104 sets of C/M phrases in total, and each condition included 26 trials. The target phrase was always made of the number 1 and a C/M word. The answer and distractor phrases each had the number 1, a C/M word and a noun. The answer and distractor differed only in their C/M word. Because the number word was the same, people could not use the number to decide. They had to treat the C/M word as a C/M word. By making the answer and distractor a minimal pair, two phrases that are almost identical except for one part, we kept the meaning of the C/M word tightly fixed (Table 3). We recorded each person's answer and their reaction time, which is how long they took to respond.

**Table 3.** How the phrases were built, with one example set for each condition.

| Type of word | Value type | Target C/M | C/M Option 1 | C/M Option 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number word | Fixed | 一副 yi fu one set of (M1, n = 2) | 一對耳環 yi dui erhuan one pair of earrings (M1, n = 2) | 一只耳環 yi zhi erhuan one earring (C, n = 1) |
| | Variable | 一隊 yi dui one team of (M2, n > 1) | 一群殺手 yi qun shashou one group of killers (M2, n > 1) | 一幫殺手 yi bang shashou one gang of killers (M2, n > 1) |
| Non-number word | Fixed | 一公斤 yi gongjin one kilo of (M3) | 一磅橡膠 yi bang xiangjiao one pound of rubber (M3) | 一噸橡膠 yi dun xiangjiao one ton of rubber (M3) |
| | Variable | 一杯 yi bei one cup of (M4) | 一罐咖啡 yi guan kafei one can of coffee (M4) | 一瓶咖啡 yi ping kafei one bottle of coffee (M4) |

There were 26 trials for each condition. In each trial, people saw three C/M phrases on the screen: a target phrase at the top, an answer phrase and a distractor phrase at the bottom. The target phrase was made of the number 1 and a C/M word. The answer and distractor formed a minimal pair, each with the number 1, a C/M word and a noun. In this table, the answer phrases are shown in bold. In the experiment, they were not shown in bold.

### How the experiment ran

We started with eight practice trials so that everyone fully understood the task. In each trial, three C/M phrases appeared on the screen, one at each corner of a triangle (Fig 1). People had to compare how close the meanings were. They had to choose which of the two phrases at the bottom was closer in meaning to the target phrase at the top. We shuffled the positions of the answer and the distractor. People had up to 8 seconds to respond, and there was a 500-millisecond pause between trials.

There were 104 trials in total, with 26 in each condition, and we shuffled the order of the trials. Right after the experiment, each person filled in a questionnaire about the mathematical values they personally felt the M2 and M4 words carried. The questionnaire listed every C/M word from the experiment in the form [one C/M word]. For example, for yi fu (one set of), a person had to fill in the blank "yue 'ge' (around 'C')" to show the value they felt it carried.

For the non-number words M3 and M4, people had to fill in the blank with about how much they thought each word stood for, in centimeters for length, square meters for area, grams for weight and milliliters for volume. For example, when they saw yi bei (one cup of), they had to fill in the blank "yue 'haosheng' (around 'milliliter')" to show the value they felt it carried.

**Fig 1.** How the experiment ran.

In each trial, people saw three C/M phrases on the screen. They had to choose between the two at the bottom the one closer in meaning to the target phrase at the top. The two choices were minimal pairs: they had the same number word, the same classifier or measure word, and the same noun.

### How we analysed the data

We analysed the answers and reaction times with a two-way repeated measures ANOVA. This is a statistical test that checks whether two factors, here the type of word (number word or non-number word) and the value type (fixed or variable), affect people's answers. "Repeated measures" means the test takes into account that the same people answered every version of the experiment. We ran it in the program IBM SPSS 20.0 and set the cut-off for statistical significance at .05. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

After this, we looked more closely at each factor on its own, using t-tests, which compare the averages of two groups. Because we made several comparisons, we applied Bonferroni's correction. This makes the test stricter, so that chance results are less likely to slip through when many comparisons are made.

We also worked out how accurate people were with M2 and M4. To do this, we used the personal mathematical values each person reported (see S1 Table for summary numbers). For each person, we decided which answer was correct in each trial based on the values they had given. Take the M2 example in Table 3. Suppose a person said that yi dui (one team of) carried a value of 10, yi qun (one group of) a value of 20, and yi bang (one gang of) a value of 30. Then, for this person, the correct answer in that trial would be yi qun shashou (one group of killers), not yi bang shashou (one gang of killers), because 20 is closer to 10 than 30 is.
parts.results:
## Results

Table 4 shows the average accuracy and the average reaction time (RT) for each group of phrases. It also gives the standard deviation (SD) in brackets. The standard deviation tells you how spread out the people's answers were around the average.

**Table 4.** Average accuracy (the share of answers that were correct) and average reaction time (RT, in seconds) in the experiment. The number in brackets is the standard deviation (SD).

| | Numerical C/M | Non-numerical C/M |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed value** | | |
| Accuracy (proportion correct) | 0.734 (0.086) | 0.744 (0.079) |
| RT (s) | 2.446 (0.634) | 2.511 (0.585) |
| **Variable value** | | |
| Accuracy (proportion correct) | 0.568 (0.130) | 0.583 (0.124) |
| RT (s) | 2.794 (0.708) | 2.886 (0.666) |

### Accuracy

We looked at two things that could affect accuracy. The first was the kind of word: a numerical word, which carries a number, or a non-numerical word, which does not. The second was the mathematical value: fixed or variable. We also checked for an interaction between the two. An interaction would mean that the effect of one thing depends on the other. For example, the gap between fixed and variable values might be bigger for one kind of word than for the other.

To test these effects, we used a statistical method called analysis of variance (ANOVA). It gives a test score, written F, that gets bigger the more clearly the groups differ. The numbers in brackets after F, here (1,19), describe how much information went into the test. The p-value tells us how often a difference this large would turn up by chance alone if there were really no difference. We call a result statistically significant when p is below .05. That means a gap this large would appear by chance less than 5% of the time if there were really no difference.

The kind of word did not have a statistically significant effect on accuracy, F (1,19) = .227, p = .639. In other words, we could not show a difference between the numerical words and the non-numerical words. The numerical words were the classifiers (C) and measure words (M1 and M2) that carry a number. The non-numerical words were the measure words M3 and M4.

The mathematical value, however, did have a statistically significant effect, F (1,19) = 68.298, p < .001. People were significantly more accurate with classifiers and measure words that have a fixed value than with those whose value can vary. Looking at the two kinds of word separately, people were significantly more accurate with C and M1 than with M2 (p < .001). They were also significantly more accurate with M3 than with M4 (p < .001). There was no significant interaction between the kind of word and the mathematical value, F (1,19) = .013, p = .91 (Table 4).

### Reaction times

The kind of word did not have a statistically significant effect on reaction time, F (1,19) = 2.098, p = .164. So we could not show a difference in speed between the numerical words (C and M1–2) and the non-numerical words (M3–4).

The mathematical value did have a statistically significant effect, F (1,19) = 37.726, p < .001. People answered faster when they processed classifiers and measure words with a fixed value than when they processed those with a variable value. People were significantly faster with C and M1 than with M2 (p = .001). They were also significantly faster with M3 than with M4 (p < .001). There was no interaction between the kind of word and the mathematical value, F (1,19) = .068, p = .797 (Table 4).

Overall, reaction times followed the same pattern as accuracy across the four groups. The more accurate people were, the faster they answered.
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

Our results showed that people judged how close two phrases were in meaning by using the mathematical values of the classifiers and measure words. This was true whether or not those values were written as numbers. It held when the values were fixed, but not when they could vary. People also answered faster when the values were fixed than when they varied.

With varying values, people were not very accurate. On average, they were right about 56.8% of the time for measure words (M2) and 58.3% of the time for sortal classifiers (M4). That is only slightly better than guessing. We worked out each person's accuracy separately, based on the mathematical values that each person told us they had in mind. This fits what we predicted: classifiers and measure words with fixed values can be compared mathematically, while those with varying values are too vague to compare.

It is still possible that people held a rough value for M2 or M4 in their minds and tried to compare it. But because these values vary, people may not have held them in exactly the same way every time. In other words, the values they had in mind may have shifted between the moment they did the meaning-comparison task and the moment they filled in the questionnaire at the end. To fix this weakness, we suggest that future studies ask people to report the values they had in mind right after each trial.

It is worth noting that the average value people had in mind for M2 ranged only from 5 to 18, and the spread was fairly small (see S1 Table). This may have made it hard to choose between the two options, so people may have been about as likely as a coin toss to pick either one. Even if people did hold a mathematical value for M2, the two options may have been so close that there was no clear difference between them. For M4, the average value people had in mind varied more than it did for M2, but the spread was large. This shows that people differed a lot from one another in the values they had in mind for M4.

We suggest that future studies use a complete sentence or story to set the context, so that the meaning of the classifiers and measure words is more tightly controlled. Our people's answers could not tell us whether they handled classifiers and measure words with varying values mathematically. Future studies could look into this with fMRI, a brain scan that shows which parts of the brain are active. They could check for activity in areas linked to handling numbers, such as the IPS, a region in the brain that helps with numbers [11–12].

Someone might argue that a "gang" of killers could mean a different number of people than a "gang" of hooligans. In the same way, a "litter" of mice might mean a different number than a "litter" of cats. This may indeed be true for M2 and M4, whose values vary. Yet this possible effect of the noun did not play a part in our experiment. Every pair we compared, made up of one M2 or M4 and one noun, used exactly the same noun.

Someone might also suspect that how easy these pairs are to tell apart could change from one noun to another. For example, the difference between a "team" of salespeople and a "gang" of salespeople might differ, not only in size but even in direction, from the difference between a "team" of killers and a "gang" of killers. Again, this possible effect did not play a part in our experiment. We never asked people to compare across pairs. We only asked them to compare within each pair.

As we expected, we found no statistically significant difference between classifiers and measure words whose values were written as numbers and those whose values were not. (A difference is called statistically significant when a gap that large would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no difference. "Not significant" means we could not show a difference, not that there is none.) One reason may be the kind of task we used, in which people compared how close two phrases were in meaning. People probably turned the phrase without a number into the same unit so they could compare it. For example, when people had to choose between yi bang (a pound) and yi gongjin (one kilo), they probably turned them into 453 grams and 1000 grams, whether exactly or roughly, before making their choice.

In other words, because this kind of task may require comparing amounts accurately, people may have preferred to turn classifiers and measure words into numbers to do it. This may explain why we did not find a significant difference between the two kinds. We suggest that future studies use other tasks to find out whether people handle the two kinds in the same way, whatever the task. Future studies could also use brain scans to see whether the two kinds use the same network of brain areas.

Our results partly support our idea that classifiers and measure words carry mathematical values. We found that people did hold and compare the mathematical values of those with fixed values. If people had not handled them by their mathematical values, people would not have been right more often than chance would allow for the phrases with numbers. However, it is still unclear how people handled classifiers and measure words with varying values. We also do not know whether people turned phrases without numbers into numbers to do the meaning-comparison task. So future studies need to look more closely at how people handle these phrases without numbers, using other tasks.

Overall, our findings partly support Her's [8] mathematical theory of classifiers and measure words, which says that these words carry mathematical values. We showed this with evidence from people's behaviour for classifiers and measure words with fixed mathematical values.

As far as we know, this is the first study to show that Chinese classifiers and measure words carry mathematical values. People held and compared the fixed mathematical values of these words to judge how close two phrases were in meaning. This finding gives real-world evidence for Her's [8] mathematical theory. In that theory, the classifier (C) and the measure word (M) come together as the multiplicand of the number (Num), meaning the number is multiplied by them. But they differ in their own values: C = 1, while M is not 1. We confirmed the idea that sortal classifiers carry the value 1 and measure words carry other mathematical values. We did this by showing that, when the mathematical values were fixed, people chose the classifier or measure word whose value was the same as, or closer to, the one in the target phrase.

Future studies of language, both in the mind and in the brain, should look further into whether the mathematical link between the number and the classifier or measure word is multiplication. In short, our findings suggest that the way Chinese uses classifiers and measure words might shape how people think about size and amount.
